This may reflect a more subtle and progressive inflammatory process, in contrast to acute destructive damage seen in post-infectious etiologies [15,16,17,26] (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Single axial thin-slice (1 mm) chest CT in lung windows from a human patient. The caption explicitly attributes the scan to a subject with type ZZ alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency and states it shows bronchiectasis in the lower lung lobes with no emphysema. Visually, the lower lobes (especially the right lower lobe) demonstrate dilated thick-walled bronchi with ring shadows and tram-track opacities consistent with cylindrical/varicose bronchiectasis, matching the captioned finding. This is a real patient radiology image of a specific clinical manifestation of the configured target disease, so it is included. Bronchiectasis is a recognized but less common association than the classic basal panacinar emphysema, hence variant typicality; the in-text note that the association is hard to prove slightly tempers confidence but does not negate the explicit caption attribution. [raw subtype: ZZ]

plate_findings.evidence: advanced panacinar destruction of the lung parenchyma

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Genuine patient H&E lung histology explicitly captioned as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency emphysema, showing advanced panacinar destruction of lung parenchyma with macrophage accumulation—the hallmark panacinar emphysema of AATD; in-text confirms these findings in AATD cases (Fig. 1A). B: Genuine patient PAS-stained lung histology explicitly captioned as showing severe acute and chronic bronchiolitis in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; bronchiolitis is a recognized pulmonary manifestation of AATD and the in-text confirms it in all AATD cases (Fig. 1B). No vocabulary key exists for bronchiolitis, so it is recorded as a proposed finding.

panels.figure_caption: Histology of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency emphysema. In alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, advanced panacinar destruction of the lung parenchyma and accumulation of macrophages (A, hematoxylin eosin, original magnification ×40), as well as severe acute and chronic bronchiolitis are seen (B, periodic acid Schiff's reaction, original magnification ×100).
in_text_mentions: The median value of age was 46.5 in AATD, 58.0 in non-AATD emphysema and 64.5 in hamartochondroma. The rate of females varied between 33.3% in AATD, 37.5% in non-AATD and 42.9% in hamartochondroma. Histology revealed destruction of the alveoli, intra-alveolar accumulation of macrophages, and acute alongside chronic bronchiolitis in all cases of AATD (Fig. 1A,1B) and non-AATD emphysema (Fig. 2A,2B) consistent with previous examinations. In cases of hamartochondroma only some macrophages and mucus in the bronchioli could be detected (Fig. 3).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Genuine HRCT axial section at the carina in an elderly patient with confirmed AATD. Shows diffuse panlobular (panacinar) emphysema with lobular destruction, the classic CT manifestation of AATD, plus a right lower lobe consolidation (community-acquired pneumonia). Real patient radiology directly supporting the target disease. B: Caudal HRCT axial section in the same elderly AATD patient. Shows marked basal-predominant panacinar emphysema with thin residual alveolar septa and bronchial wall thickening, a textbook CT presentation of AATD. in_text_mentions: High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest confirmed extensive bilateral panlobular emphysema with a predominantly basal and central distribution (Figure 2A), along with a right lower lobe consolidation (Figure 2B). Sputum and blood cultures were negative. The patient improved clinically and was discharged on LTOT, oral corticosteroids, oral antibiotics, and inhaled bronchodilators, with a working diagnosis of acute-on-chronic type II respiratory failure secondary to community-acquired pneumonia.
